title: Pirkei Avot
hookLine: a short tractate of sayings, read on summer Shabbat afternoons for centuries

cards: Something a grandmother said at a kitchen table. A line from a coach. A sticky note on the fridge that's been there so long it's gone yellow.
A few sentences like that can carry a person a long way. They're short, portable, and they show up when they're needed. Jewish tradition has a whole little book of those sentences.
You could read it in an afternoon. And an afternoon is when it's customarily read: on Saturday afternoons, in the long, slow light of summer.

teach.b: It's called Pirkei Avot: chapters of the fathers, or, as it's often called in English, the Ethics of the Fathers. Avot, fathers, means the founding teachers, the sages who shaped Jewish life.

It's part of the Mishnah, the great collection of Jewish oral law, gathered, tradition says, by Rabbi Judah the Prince. The Mishnah is mostly law: how to keep the Sabbath, how to settle a lawsuit, how to plant a field.

teach.h: A MISHNAH WITH ALMOST NO LAW.
teach.b: Almost no law at all, just sayings passed from teacher to student, each with the teacher's name attached.
And a curious detail: the rabbis didn't place it in the section about prayer or holidays, but in the section on damages and courts. One explanation: the people who judge others most need to hear it.

A custom grew of reading one chapter each Shabbat afternoon between Passover and Shavuot, six chapters, one Sabbath at a time. Some communities keep going all summer, around and around, until the fall holidays.
It's printed in traditional prayer books, and you may already know a line from it without knowing where it came from. Hillel's three questions, for example: if I'm not for myself, who will be?
If I'm only for myself, what am I?
And if not now, when? That's Avot. Over the next weeks, you'll read it the way it's meant to be read: one saying at a time, slowly.

how: A chapter of Pirkei Avot is customarily studied each Shabbat afternoon from Passover, in some communities through the summer; each chapter is traditionally introduced with the line that all Israel has a share in the world to come.

practice: Take Hillel's three questions one at a time, letting each one sit: if I'm not for myself, who will be? If I'm only for myself, what am I? If not now, when?
Don't answer them; just turn each one over, the way you'd turn a stone in your hand.
